name: Anub
title: Son of Kos in the tribe of Judah
summary: In the genealogy of the tribe of Judah in 1 Chronicles, Anub appears as a son of Kos and sibling of Zobeba. He belongs to a branch of the tribe of Judah where several names carry possible botanical connotations – his father's name Kos means "thorn," while Anub's own name is linked by some scholars to the Hebrew word for "grape," although the etymology remains disputed. No stories or actions are connected with Anub in the biblical text, but his presence in the genealogy highlights how the family lists in Chronicles carefully documented each family's belonging within God's covenant people. Such registers had practical and theological significance by confirming inheritance rights, tribal affiliation, and continuity in God's redemptive history.

keyEvents.description: Anub is mentioned as the son of Kos, along with his sibling Zobeba, in the genealogical record of the tribe of Judah in 1 Chronicles.

versions.summary: Anub is a person mentioned in 1 Chronicles as a descendant of Judah through Kos. He is known only from a genealogy and plays no prominent narrative role in the Bible. His name appears in connection with the genealogies of the tribe of Judah.

versions.reason: [major] Anub is a descendant of Judah mentioned in the genealogies in 1 Chronicles 4. These genealogies trace back to the early tribes of Israel. Although 1 Chronicles was written later, the individuals in the genealogies are typically placed in patriarchal or early Israelite times. 'divided-kingdom' is the wrong era; 'patriarchs' or 'judges' would have been more appropriate. 'Patriarchs' is chosen here since it concerns early family lines from Judah.; [minor] The roles array is empty. versions.reason: [minor] The summary is very similar to version 1 (which received a score of 5). It should be rephrased to provide a fresher and more informative text that clearly differs from the previous version.; [major] The term 'patriarchs' is somewhat imprecise for Anub. The genealogies in 1 Chronicles 4 place these family lines in a broader context. Kos and Anub likely belong to a period closer to the settlement of the land or the time of the judges, not the patriarchal era (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob). 'Judges' or 'conquest' would have been more appropriate.; [minor] The verse mentioned is 1 Chron 4:8, but it is important to verify that this is correct. In most translations, it is 1 Chron 4:8 that mentions Kos as the father of Anub and Zobeba. This appears to be correct.; [minor] 1 Chron 4:8 also mentions the descendants of Aharhel, son of Harum. It may be worth considering whether 'siblings' should include more individuals, but 'Zobeba' is the most direct relative mentioned alongside Anub.

versions.summary: Anub is mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah in 1 Chronicles as the son of Kos and brother of Zobeba. Beyond this genealogical placement, we have no further information about him. The genealogies in Chronicles were compiled to map out the history and identity of the tribes, and even brief entries like this one served an important function: they confirmed family lines, inheritance rights, and each family's place within God's covenant people. Anub's name, which possibly has a botanical meaning related to grapes, is part of a series of plant-associated names in this section of the genealogical record.

Many of the names in these lists may belong to different periods. 'judges' is a reasonable assumption, but 'united-kingdom' or even another epoch could also be defended. footnotes.text: The name Anub (Hebrew: עֲנוּב, 'Anuv) has an uncertain etymology. Some scholars link it to the root ענב ('anav), meaning "grape," viewing it as a name with agricultural associations. Others suggest a connection to the root ענה, which can mean "to answer" or "to be humble." The exact meaning remains debated.

The genealogies in 1 Chronicles 2–4 served as important identity documents for the tribe of Judah, especially in the period after the Babylonian exile. These lists were used to confirm land rights, tribal affiliation, and cultic legitimacy. Even individuals like Anub, who have no narrative role, contributed to documenting the complete family history of the tribe.

Kos (Hebrew: קוֹץ, Qots), Anub's father, means "thorn" or "thornbush." Several names in this part of the genealogy have botanical associations, which may reflect the agricultural culture of the Judah region and the symbolic significance that plant names held in Semitic naming traditions.

The geographical area associated with the clans of the tribe of Judah in 1 Chronicles 4 largely encompasses the Shephelah region and the Negev. Archaeological findings from these areas show settlements from the Iron Age that correspond to the tribal structures described in the genealogies.

In rabbinic tradition, the genealogies in the Books of Chronicles are subject to extensive commentary. The Talmud (Pesachim 62b) refers to a 'Chronicles midrash' that interpreted these family records allegorically and spiritually, although details about exactly Anub are not preserved in known rabbinic sources.
